entries.description:
What a document's write does: the first argument of a document object's Write, and the second parameter of its BeforeWrite handler - `BeforeWrite(Cancel, WriteMode, PostingMode)` in the object module, `BeforeWrite(Source, Cancel, WriteMode, PostingMode)` in an event handler. Write with no argument is DocumentWriteMode.Write.

Posting runs the Posting handler and writes the movements it fills; UndoPosting runs the UndoPosting handler and clears them; Write saves the document and leaves its posted mark as it is. All three run in one transaction: a handler that sets Cancel, or a movement that fails, leaves the document as it was.
entries.example:
Doc.Write(DocumentWriteMode.Posting);       // save and post
Doc.Write(DocumentWriteMode.UndoPosting);   // clear the movements, keep the document
Doc.Write();                                // save, posted mark unchanged

entries.description: Save the document and post it: the Posting handler fills the movements and they are written with the document, which is then marked Posted. Posting a posted document again first clears its previous movements, as RegisterRecordsDeletion says.
Save the document and undo its posting: the UndoPosting handler runs, the movements are cleared (unless RegisterRecordsDeletion is Never) and the Posted mark is taken off.
Save the document only. Its posted mark and its movements stay as they are. The default of Write().

How a posting is meant: as the event happens (RealTime) or as an entry made after it (Regular). The second argument of a document object's Write - left out, RealTime - and the parameter the BeforeWrite and Posting handlers receive (`Posting(Cancel, PostingMode)`).

The platform posts the same way under both and only hands the mode on: what differs is the handler's to decide - typically, real time checks stock against the balance as it stands now. The form's Post commands, marking a document for deletion and reposting through a sequence write with Regular.
The posting happens as the event does - a sale at the till. The default of a document object's Write.
An entry made after the event - a document of the past, a reposting. What the form's Post commands and the platform's own repostings use.

What the platform does with a document's movements when it is posted again or its posting is undone: the document's RegisterRecordsDeletion property, set in the designer. A script reads it off the metadata - `Metadata.Documents.<Name>.RegisterRecordsDeletion`. A deleted document takes its movements with it whatever this says.
The default. The previous posting's movements are cleared before the Posting handler runs, so it writes them from nothing, and cleared when the posting is undone.
Kept when the document is posted again - a record set the handler writes replaces its own - and cleared when the posting is undone.
The platform never clears them on posting or undoing it: the configuration's Posting and UndoPosting handlers do.

When a document's numbers start again: the document's NumberPeriodicity property, set in the designer. Periodic, the next number is the next one inside that period of the document's date, and a new period starts again at one. A script reads it off the metadata - `Metadata.Documents.<Name>.NumberPeriodicity`.
One series of numbers for the life of the document. The default; a document saved before the setting existed stays on it.
The numbers start again at one every calendar year of the document's date.
The numbers start again at one every quarter of the document's date.
The numbers start again at one every month of the document's date.
The numbers start again at one every day of the document's date.
What an accumulation register keeps: the register's RegisterType property, set in the designer. A script reads it off the metadata - `Metadata.AccumulationRegisters.<Name>.RegisterType`.
The default. Movements are receipts and expenses (their RecordType), and the register answers what stands at a moment: Balance, Turnovers, BalanceAndTurnovers.
Movements are only summed over a period - Turnovers, no balance and no RecordType.

Whether a movement of an accumulation register of balances adds its resources to the balance or takes them away: the movement's RecordType field. A new movement is a Receipt until the code says otherwise. A register of turnovers has no RecordType.

In a query it is compared like any field, the member passed as a parameter.
entries.example:
q = New Query("SELECT COUNT(*) AS N FROM AccumulationRegister.Stock AS S WHERE S.RecordType = &Kind");
q.SetParameter("Kind", AccumulationRecordType.Expense);

entries.description: The movement takes its resources away from the balance - goods shipped, money paid out.
The movement adds its resources to the balance - goods received, money paid in. What a new movement is until the code says otherwise.

The side of the account a line moves, in an accounting register WITHOUT correspondence (one side per line): the line's RecordType field. A new line is Debit until the code says otherwise; the record set's AddDebit and AddCredit add a line with its side already set. In a register with correspondence the side is said by which account a line fills, and AddDebit / AddCredit add an ordinary line.
The line moves the debit side of its account. What a new line is until the code says otherwise; AddDebit sets it.
The line moves the credit side of its account; AddCredit sets it.

The side of an account's balance: the AccountType attribute every account of a chart of accounts carries, read as `Account.AccountType` off a reference or an account object. Required - every posting asks which side an amount moves; a new account is Active.
The account's balance is a debit. What a new account is.
The account's balance is a credit.
The balance may fall either way and is shown as it falls - a settlements account.

Whether an information register's values have a history, and at what grain: the register's Periodicity property, set in the designer. Periodic, records carry a Period truncated to that grain - one record per set of dimensions per period - and SliceLast / SliceFirst read the value as of a moment. A script reads it off the metadata - `Metadata.InformationRegisters.<Name>.Periodicity`.
No history: one value per set of dimensions, and no Period. The default.
A record's Period keeps the date to the second.
A record's Period is the start of its day: one record per key per day.
A record's Period is the start of its month: one record per key per month.
A record's Period is the start of its quarter: one record per key per quarter.
A record's Period is the start of its year: one record per key per year.
Who writes an information register's records: the register's WriteMode property, set in the designer. A script reads it off the metadata - `Metadata.InformationRegisters.<Name>.WriteMode`.
The default. Records are written on their own, by key, from the record form or from code; the register has a record manager.
Records are movements of documents: written and cleared with their recorder, like an accumulation register's.

The grain of a calculation register's registration period: the register's Periodicity property, set in the designer. A record is registered for the start of the period its date falls in. A script reads it off the metadata - `Metadata.CalculationRegisters.<Name>.Periodicity`.
Records are registered for a day.
Records are registered for a month. The default.
Records are registered for a quarter.
Records are registered for a year.

Which period of a base record puts it into a base - what a calculation register's GetBase reads: the BaseDependence property of a chart of calculation types, set in the designer. A script reads it off the metadata - `Metadata.ChartsOfCalculationTypes.<Name>.BaseDependence`.
The chart's types take no base at all. The default.
A base record counts for the days it is in force inside the base period, prorated.
A base record counts whole when it is registered inside the base period.

How the values of a catalog or a chart (of accounts, of characteristic types, of calculation types) are arranged: its HierarchyType property, set in the designer. It decides what Parent may point to and whether IsFolder exists. A script reads it off the metadata - `Metadata.Catalogs.<Name>.HierarchyType`.
No hierarchy: no Parent at all, a flat list.
Every value is an item and any item may stand under another - a tree without folders, as in a chart of accounts.
Folders hold items and other folders, and the list walks them as a tree. The default.

How a reference to an item reads wherever it is shown - a field, a list, a report: the DataPresentation property of a catalog or a chart, set in the designer. A script reads it off the metadata - `Metadata.Catalogs.<Name>.DataPresentation`.
A reference reads as the item's Description. The default for a catalog.
A reference reads as the item's Code. The default for a chart of accounts, whose accounts are named by their numbers.

In a catalog with folders: which nodes carry an attribute or a tabular section - the ItemMode property of the attribute or the tabular section, set in the designer. A folder's form and record show only what folders use. A script can name the members, but no object a script holds hands one out: the metadata a script reads lists no attributes.
entries.example: Message(ItemMode.Folders);   // its caption, in the user's language

entries.description: Only items carry it. The default.
Only folders carry it.
Folders and items both carry it.

Whether the database keeps an index on an attribute: the attribute's Indexing property, set in the designer. Index what searches, filters and joins go by; an index slows writes and grows the base. A script can name the members, but no object a script holds hands one out: the metadata a script reads lists no attributes.
entries.example: Message(IndexingMode.IndexWithAdditionalOrder);   // its caption, in the user's language

entries.description: No index - cheaper writes. The default.
An index on the attribute: searches and filters by it stop scanning the table.
The index also carries the object's main order, so a list filtered by the attribute pages without sorting.

For a field that refers to a hierarchical catalog: what may be chosen into it - the attribute's Select property, set in the designer, which the field's choice form obeys. A script can name the members, but no object a script holds hands one out: the metadata a script reads lists no attributes.
entries.example: Message(SelectMode.Folders);   // its caption, in the user's language

entries.description: Only items may be chosen. The default.
Only folders may be chosen.
Folders and items may both be chosen.

Where a command group the configuration declares is shown: the group's Category property, set in the designer. A script can name the members, but no object a script holds hands one out: the metadata a script reads lists no command groups.
entries.example: Message(CommandGroupCategory.ActionsPanel);   // its caption, in the user's language

entries.description: The navigation panel of a section, beside the platform's Important and Normal groups. The default.
The actions panel of a section, beside the platform's Create, Reports and Service groups.
The command bar of a form, as one button that opens a submenu of the group's commands - the object's own and the common commands typed for that object.

The platform's own command groups of a section page, by name and caption: Important and Normal in the navigation panel, Create, Reports and Service in the actions panel. A command's Group property, set in the designer, picks one of them or a group the configuration declares. A script can name the members, but no object a script holds hands one out.
entries.example: Message(CommandInterfaceArea.Reports);   // its caption, in the user's language

entries.description: The navigation panel's top group, shown first.
The navigation panel's ordinary group. Where a command goes by default.
The actions panel's group of commands that create something.
The actions panel's group of reports.
The actions panel's group of service commands.

How a role combines with the user's other roles: the role's CompositionMode property, set in the designer. The verdict is (permitting OR permitting ...) AND restricting AND restricting ..., so the order roles are assigned in never matters. A script can name the members, but no object a script holds hands one out: the metadata a script reads lists no roles. The members' captions are Permitting and Restricting.
entries.example: Message(RoleCompositionMode.Intersection);   // its caption, in the user's language

entries.description: Permitting: the role adds rights, and one permitting role granting a right is enough. The default.

Restricting: the role grants nothing and subtracts - what it denies stays denied whatever the permitting roles grant. A data separator (an organisation, a division) is declared this way once instead of copied into every role.

The compatibility version a configuration asks for: the Version property of the configuration, set in the designer. It has one member today, and no behaviour is switched by it yet. A script can name the member, but no object a script holds hands one out.
entries.example: Message(ProgramVersion.OES_Last);   // its caption, in the user's language

entries.description: Don't use compatibility: the configuration runs the current behaviour. The default.

The dialect a configuration's modules are written in: the Syntax property of the configuration, set in the designer. The members are spelled in lower case, and the word-based dialect's is `vbs` (it reads as "ves"), the stored name kept for configurations saved before the dialect was renamed. A script can name the members, but no object a script holds hands one out.
VES, the word-based dialect - `If ... Then ... EndIf`, `While ... Do ... EndDo` - kept for migrated configurations.
CES, braces and semicolons - `if (...) { ... }`. The default for a new configuration.
